fatal_errors: The proposed coherent-nanoprecipitate mechanism is absent from the target as-cast WTaTiVZr alloy, whose relevant structure is a segregated two-BCC-phase dendritic microstructure.

The proposed 600–1200 °C irradiated plasma-facing regime does not match the tested room-temperature-to-500 °C quasi-static and indentation conditions; irradiation and reactor service were not evaluated.

The cited precipitate evidence concerns an FCC Co-Cr-Ni medium-entropy alloy at ambient temperature and does not establish precipitate-assisted climb, plasticity, or toughness in tungsten-based refractory alloys.
Thermomechanical processing and aging would also alter grain size, dislocation density, segregation, and residual stress, so the proposed comparison does not isolate precipitate density or coherency.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad goal of improving plastic strain and toughness in fusion-relevant refractory materials, and it proposes measurable mechanical and microscopy comparisons. However, it does not reconstruct the target material, intervention, conditions, structural mediator, or mechanism. The target attributes strength mainly to multicomponent solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and W/Ta-related frictional resistance, while Ti/V/Zr and the two-phase segregated structure are interpreted as aiding plasticity and crack resistance. The generated answer instead introduces engineered coherent precipitates and untested radiation conditions. Its predicted direction of improved ductility and toughness is only generically consistent. The same-composition control is preferable to an unrelated baseline, but processing-induced covariates prevent clean causal isolation. Most importantly, the cited studies do not validate the claimed high-temperature climb/glide mechanism in tungsten or refractory HEAs, making this an insufficiently supported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
